novedades.titulo: Integrated algorithm — GLP-1/GIP and reproductive planning
novedades.fuentes: Synthesis of the guides in this same section: Contraception during tirzepatide, Preconception washout by molecule, Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide, Metformin in pregnancy, GLP-1 and fertility recovery
novedades.texto: Branch 1 — Patient on GLP-1/GIP treatment who is NOT seeking pregnancy (or has not yet decided): Active contraceptive counseling from the start of treatment, even if she previously had anovulation due to PMOS (see the GLP-1 and fertility recovery guide) — fertility can recover before the patient notices. Prefer non-oral methods (LARC, injectable, patch, ring), especially with tirzepatide; if she uses an oral method, add a barrier method for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose escalation (see the Contraception during tirzepatide guide). Branch 2 — Patient who IS seeking pregnancy (preconception planning): Washout by molecule before attempting to conceive (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide) — semaglutide ≥2 months, tirzepatide ≥1 month (European/UK label), extended-release exenatide ≥3 months; no validated interval for liraglutide, dulaglutide, short-acting exenatide or lixisenatide; retatrutide does not apply, as it is not approved. Reassess baseline metabolic management (metformin, myo-inositol) in a preconception context, not a weight-loss one (see the Metformin in pregnancy and Myo-inositol guides). Preconception folic acid according to risk level (see the Preconception screening and folic acid guide). Branch 3 — Inadvertent pregnancy already confirmed during GLP-1/GIP use: Stop the drug immediately. Reassess the metabolic plan in a pregnancy context, not a weight-loss one (see the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide). Discuss the available evidence with the patient — reassuring regarding malformations, more mixed regarding gestational weight gain/gestational diabetes/hypertension (see the same guide) — without creating unwarranted alarm or false reassurance. 5 key messages for counseling: GLP-1/GIP-slowed gastric emptying can reduce absorption of oral contraceptives — discuss it proactively, not reactively. Fertility recovery from weight loss can occur before the patient notices the menstrual change. Preconception washout varies by molecule — there is no single rule for "the GLP-1s." Facing an inadvertent pregnancy, stopping the drug is the immediate step — evidence on malformations is reassuring so far, but evidence on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes is more mixed and warrants active pregnancy follow-up, not just reassurance. The real teratogen in diabetes is uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not the drug itself — do not stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan.

novedades.fuentes: AACE/ACE · Endocrine Society · SURMOUNT/STEP · Austin GO, et al. Front Mol Biosci 2023;10:1170181 · Davies M, et al. Lancet 2021;397(10278):971-984 · Rubino D, et al. JAMA 2021;325(14):1414-1425 (STEP 4) · Aronne LJ, et al. JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48 (SURMOUNT-4) · Castaneda R, et al. The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128. doi:10.1016/S3050-5038(25)00145-1 · Wilding JPH, et al. Diabetes Obes Metab 2022;24(8):1553-1564 (STEP 1 extension)
novedades.texto: Semaglutide 0.25→2.4mg/wk. Tirzepatide 2.5→10-15mg/wk. Indication: BMI≥30, or ≥27+comorbidity. ⚠️ "Ozempic babies" (restores ovulation), reduces OCP efficacy, stop before trying to conceive according to the molecule (semaglutide ≥2 months; tirzepatide ≥1 month per the European/UK label; see Preconception washout by molecule guide), risk of sarcopenia. Non-response rates (<5% weight loss) by pivotal trial: STEP-1 (semaglutide 2.4mg, non-diabetic adults) 13.6% · STEP-TEENS (semaglutide 2.4mg, adolescents with excess-weight comorbidity) 27% · SURMOUNT-1 (tirzepatide 15mg, non-diabetic adults) 9% · STEP-2 (semaglutide 2.4mg, diabetic adults) 31.2% — response is consistently lower in patients with concomitant type 2 diabetes, a point to anticipate when counseling on expectations. Maintaining weight loss requires continuing the medication (STEP 4 with semaglutide and SURMOUNT-4 with tirzepatide): in both trials, patients who, on reaching a weight-loss plateau, were randomized to continue the drug maintained or further deepened their weight loss, while those switched to placebo progressively regained weight over the remaining follow-up — obesity behaves here as a chronic condition requiring sustained treatment, not as a short course with a permanent outcome. Figures: STEP 4 (Rubino 2021), weeks 20-68: −7.9% with semaglutide vs. +6.9% with placebo; SURMOUNT-4 (Aronne, JAMA 2024;331(1):38-48), weeks 36-88: −5.5% with tirzepatide vs. +14.0% with placebo. STEP 1 extension (Wilding, Diabetes Obes Metab 2022; n=327): after −17.3% at week 68, stopping led to regain of 11.6 percentage points by week 120, about two-thirds of the weight lost. GLP-1/GIP + hormone therapy in the climacteric (retrospective cohort, Mayo Clinic): Castaneda et al. (The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology, & Women's Health. 2026;2(2):e118-e128), in 120 postmenopausal women with overweight/obesity on tirzepatide (40 on HRT vs. 80 without, propensity-matched), reported that at 15 months HRT users had 35% greater total body weight loss than non-users, along with additional cardiometabolic improvements in both groups. ⚠️ This is retrospective matched-cohort evidence, not a randomized trial — it suggests a possible synergy but does not establish causality, nor does it by itself change the indication for HRT, which should be decided on its own criteria (see the MRS Scale and HRT guide). Note: the preliminary figure presented at the ENDO 2025 congress (~17% vs. 14%) differs from the final Lancet publication — this guide uses the final published figure (35% relative difference), not the preliminary congress figure.

novedades.titulo: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraception
novedades.fuentes: CDC US MEC 2024 · WHO MEC 6th ed. (2025) · SIC 2025 · FSRH (2017, amended 2023)
novedades.texto: Categories: 1 no restriction · 2 advantages generally outweigh risks · 3 risks generally outweigh advantages (only if no other method is available or acceptable, with follow-up) · 4 unacceptable risk, do not use. With several conditions, the highest category applies. Some conditions have one category for initiation and another for continuation. Cat 4 for combined methods (US MEC 2024): breastfeeding or postpartum under 21 days; smoker aged 35 or older with 15 or more cigarettes per day; BP 160/100 or higher or vascular disease; prior VTE with high recurrence risk (no anticoagulation or prophylactic dose); known thrombophilia; major surgery with prolonged immobilization; ischemic heart disease; stroke; complicated valvular disease; peripartum cardiomyopathy (under 6 months or moderately or severely impaired function); SLE with antiphospholipid antibodies; migraine with aura; current breast cancer; decompensated cirrhosis; hepatocellular adenoma or carcinoma; chronic kidney disease (nephrotic syndrome or dialysis); sickle cell disease; transplant with graft failure. Cat 3 to 4 by severity: multiple cardiovascular risk factors, diabetes with end-organ damage or over 20 years' duration. Progestin-only: cat 4 with current breast cancer; cat 3 with past cancer and no disease for 5 years. The 3-monthly injectable (DMPA) is cat 3 with BP 160/100 or higher, vascular disease, ischemic heart disease, stroke, high-risk VTE, thrombophilia and diabetes with end-organ damage. IUD (copper and LNG), cat 4 for initiation: pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, immediately after septic abortion, current PID or purulent cervicitis, chlamydia or gonorrhea, distorted uterine cavity, unexplained bleeding before evaluation, cervical or endometrial cancer awaiting treatment, trophoblastic disease with intrauterine disease, pelvic tuberculosis. Differences with WHO 2025 (6th ed.): progestin injectables while breastfeeding under 6 weeks moved from cat 3 to 2 and can be offered immediately after delivery; nevirapine and ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors moved to cat 1 with all hormonal methods (US MEC 2024 keeps cat 2 or 3 for some); with PrEP all methods are cat 1; repeated emergency contraception in the same cycle is cat 1; inflammatory bowel disease was added. Over 40 (SIC consensus 2025): cardiovascular safety is the main factor. Estrogen-free methods do not increase venous or arterial risk. Among combined methods, EE/levonorgestrel, EE/norgestimate and natural estradiol increase VTE the least; EE 20 µg with drospirenone and natural estradiol do not increase arterial risk. Heavy bleeding, from most to least effective: LNG-IUD 52 mg, estradiol valerate/dienogest, ring, COC with EE 30-35 µg, progestin-only. COCs protect bone; the implant, progestin-only pill and LNG-IUD are neutral. When to stop contraception (FSRH): generally at 55. Non-hormonal method: 2 years of amenorrhea under 50 and 1 year at 50 or older. Combined and DMPA: until 50, then switch method. Implant, progestin-only pill or LNG-IUD with amenorrhea from age 50: if FSH is above 30 IU/L, stop after 1 more year. FSH is not useful on combined methods or MHT. MHT can be added to a non-combined method. Other data: tirzepatide may reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives; use a non-oral method or add a barrier for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase (FDA label). The etonogestrel implant is approved for 5 years (ANMAT 2025).

novedades.titulo: Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide — what the evidence shows
novedades.fuentes: Brown ME, et al. GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use During the Periconceptional Period, Ann Intern Med (2026) — target trial emulation, n=3,572 · D'Antonio F, et al. Periconceptional and early pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists and obstetric/neonatal outcomes, Med (2026) — meta-analysis, n=2,118,215 · AJOG 2024 (review), PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0 · Uysal N, et al. Pregnancy outcomes following maternal GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sci Rep. 2026;16:31416 · Liu X, et al. Periconceptional use of GLP-1 receptor agonists and the risk of major congenital malformations: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Endocr Connect. 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280 · Maya J, et al. Gestational Weight Gain and Pregnancy Outcomes After GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Discontinuation. JAMA. 2025;334(24):2186-2196. DOI 10.1001/jama.2025.20951 · Pondugula N, et al. Gestational Weight Gain and Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy With Prepregnancy and Early Pregnancy GLP-1RA Exposure. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995
novedades.texto: Immediate management of an inadvertent pregnancy in a patient using GLP-1/GIP: Stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is confirmed — current evidence does not support continuing it during gestation, regardless of the duration of periconceptional exposure that has already occurred. Reassess the patient's overall metabolic management plan (glycemia, weight, possible metformin indication — see corresponding guide) now in the context of pregnancy, not of weight loss. There is no indication for pregnancy termination based solely on periconceptional GLP-1/GIP exposure — the conversation with the patient should be grounded in the available evidence (summarized below), which so far shows no consistent signal of harm. What the evidence shows (quick-reference summary, not a substitute for each study's methodological detail): Brown et al. (Ann Intern Med 2026, target trial emulation, n=3,572) found no significant increase in major congenital malformations associated with periconceptional exposure to GLP-1 agonists, using a design that emulates a randomized trial from observational data to reduce confounding by indication. Major congenital malformations: adjusted prevalence ratio 1.21 (95% CI 0.83-1.82); non-live birth: adjusted RR 1.09 (Ann Intern Med 2026;179(7):929-937). Wide intervals: a moderate effect cannot be excluded. D'Antonio et al. (Med 2026, large-scale meta-analysis, n=2,118,215) likewise found no consistent signal of increased risk of adverse obstetric/neonatal outcomes associated with periconceptional or early-pregnancy exposure to GLP-1/GIP agonists — this being the largest sample-size analysis available to date on the topic. The AJOG 2024 review (PII S0002-9378(24)00864-0) synthesizes the body of evidence available at that time in the same reassuring direction, although — like the rest of this literature — it is based predominantly on observational studies rather than randomized trials specifically designed to assess reproductive safety. ⚠️ All of this evidence is observational (cohorts, target trial emulation, cohort meta-analyses) — absence of a harm signal is not equivalent to definitive evidence of safety, and it does not change the recommendation to stop the drug as soon as pregnancy is recognized, nor the recommendation to respect the preconception washout by molecule when pregnancy is planned (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide). Malformations — additional meta-analysis (Uysal et al., Sci Rep 2026;16:31416): across 7 cohort studies with over 40,000 exposed pregnancies, there was no significant signal for congenital malformations overall (OR 1.11; 95% CI 0.82-1.51) nor for major malformations with first-trimester exposure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.73-2.65). An isolated significant signal was found for urinary malformations (OR 1.24; 95% CI 1.05-1.47), based on unadjusted data from only 2 studies — the authors themselves attribute it most likely to residual confounding (underlying maternal diabetes/obesity), not a direct teratogenic effect. No increased signal was found for stillbirth, spontaneous abortion, small for gestational age, or preterm birth. Major congenital malformations — largest sample-size meta-analysis available to date (Liu X, et al. Endocrine Connections 2026;15(7). DOI 10.1530/EC-26-0280): across 6 studies (1 prospective + 5 retrospective) with 286,599 women, of whom 43,577 had periconceptional GLP-1RA exposure, there was no significant difference in the risk of major congenital malformations between exposed and unexposed women (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.96-1.08). No significant signal was found either for preterm birth (RR 1.09; 95% CI 0.80-1.49), large for gestational age (RR 2.31; 95% CI 0.56-9.44), small for gestational age (RR 0.71; 95% CI 0.39-1.27), or stillbirth (RR 1.16; 95% CI 0.24-5.69) — these last three have very wide confidence intervals due to low event numbers, and should be read as "insufficient statistical power to detect a risk if one existed," not as "no risk." The authors themselves note that, given the observational design and limited number of exposed pregnancies, these findings should not be interpreted as proof of safety. Gestational weight gain and complications after stopping the drug (Maya J, et al. JAMA 2025;334(24):2186-2196 — retrospective cohort, Mass General Brigham, n=448 exposed vs. 1,344 unexposed, matched by propensity score 1:3, 84% with obesity): exposure to GLP-1/GIP between 3 years before and 90 days after conception was associated with greater gestational weight gain (mean 13.7kg vs. 10.5kg; difference +3.3kg; 95% CI 2.3-4.2; p<0.001), a higher risk of excess gestational weight gain (65% vs. 49%; RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.19-1.47), of preterm delivery (17% vs. 13%; RR 1.34; 95% CI 1.06-1.69), of gestational diabetes (20% vs. 15%; RR 1.30; 95% CI 1.01-1.68), and of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (46% vs. 36%; RR 1.29; 95% CI 1.12-1.49) — with no difference in birth length, large/small for gestational age, or cesarean delivery. ⚠️ Unlike Liu et al. (above), which looks for a malformation signal, this cohort looks at the pregnant patient's own metabolic/hypertensive outcomes after periconceptional exposure — a different, and to some extent contrasting, perspective to the reassurance conveyed by Imbroane et al. 2025 (see the Preconception washout by molecule guide): "no malformation signal" does not equal "no maternal risk at all." Cohort composed mostly of women with obesity — limits generalization to a non-obese population. Gestational weight gain and hypertensive disorders — independent cohort (Pondugula N, et al. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;147(3):293-302. DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000005995): a retrospective cohort distinct from Maya et al. (Yale, n=243 exposed up to 1 year before pregnancy — 103 for pregestational diabetes, 140 for weight management — vs. 175 and 200 unexposed, respectively). Found no association between GLP-1RA exposure and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy in either cohort (pregestational diabetes: adjusted OR 0.72; 95% CI 0.42-1.25 · weight management: adjusted OR 0.83; 95% CI 0.45-1.52). There was also no association with gestational weight gain in the pregestational diabetes cohort; in the weight-management cohort, exposure was associated with a lower likelihood of gestational weight gain below recommendations (adjusted OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.18-0.78) — the authors interpret this as a possible rebound weight gain after stopping the drug, not as excess weight gain. ⚠️ Important attribution note: the figures of 65% vs. 49% excess weight gain, 20% vs. 15% gestational diabetes, and 46% vs. 36% hypertensive disorders (above) belong to Maya et al., not to this study — these are two independent cohorts with different findings (Pondugula et al. reports no hypertensive-disorder signal; Maya et al. does).

novedades.fuentes: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee. Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026. Diabetes Care. 2026 · NICE Guideline NG3. Diabetes in pregnancy · Rowan JA, Hague WM, Gao W, et al. (MiG Trial). N Engl J Med. 2008;358(19):2003-2015 · Rowan JA, et al. (MiG TOFU, offspring follow-up at 2 and 7-9 years). Diabetes Care 2011 / BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2018 · ADA/ALAD (see Gestational Diabetes guide)
novedades.texto: The approach to metformin once pregnancy is confirmed depends on why it was prescribed — it is not a single rule: PMOS with ovulation induction/insulin resistance: ADA 2026 (recommendation 15.22, level A): when metformin was used for PCOS and ovulation induction, stop it by the end of the first trimester at the latest. Many of these patients reach pregnancy already on metformin and/or myo-inositol as part of their baseline metabolic management (see the PMOS and Myo-inositol guides) — there is no teratogenicity signal for metformin requiring its immediate discontinuation upon confirming pregnancy, unlike GLP-1/GIP analogues (see the Inadvertent pregnancy guide). Prediabetes: individualize according to glycemic control and risk factors. ADA (2026 Standards of Care) does not position metformin as routine in isolated gestational prediabetes — its use follows the same individualization logic as in non-pregnant high-risk patients (elevated BMI, prior GDM, PMOS). NICE (NG3) is somewhat more permissive when risk factors for frank gestational diabetes coexist, where metformin may be anticipated as part of early management if glycemia warrants it — neither guideline indicates it routinely in isolated prediabetes without another risk factor. ADA 2026: metformin does not prevent gestational diabetes (meta-analysis of 11 RCTs). NICE NG3 (1.1.21): metformin may be used as an adjunct or alternative to insulin before and during pregnancy when the glycemic benefit outweighs potential harm. Pregestational diabetes: ADA prioritizes insulin as first-choice treatment (type 1 and, in most cases, type 2) due to metformin's transplacental passage and a preference for more predictable control; it reserves metformin as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes with high insulin resistance/high requirements, not as monotherapy. NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as first-line or adjunctive therapy in pregestational type 2 diabetes, adding insulin if the glycemic target is not reached — a stance more favorable to oral therapy than ADA's. Gestational diabetes: metformin as a second-line agent versus insulin per ADA (insulin as the preferred first line, metformin as an acceptable alternative after discussing transplacental passage with the patient); NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as a reasonable first line before insulin, barring contraindication or lack of response — see also the algorithm already described in the Gestational Diabetes guide. Summary of the ADA vs. NICE divergence: both agree that uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not metformin, is the real teratogen, but they differ in how much weight they give oral metformin versus insulin: ADA tends to favor insulin as first-line therapy in overt diabetes (pregestational and gestational), reserving metformin as an adjunct or an alternative discussed case by case; NICE accepts metformin more broadly as a reasonable first line in several scenarios. Neither guideline diverges on PMOS, where the decision is individualized for reasons unrelated to fetal safety. Key counseling point: the demonstrated teratogen in this context is uncontrolled hyperglycemia — not metformin itself. This should guide the decision not to abruptly stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan (insulin or another scheme). Offspring follow-up (MiG TOFU): follow-up of the MiG trial children at 2 years (Diabetes Care 2011) and 7-9 years (BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2018) assessed body composition and metabolic outcomes after in-utero metformin exposure — with no signal of harm that would contraindicate its use in gestational diabetes; this is the longest-term support available for this specific indication.

novedades.titulo: Myo-inositol — PMOS, ovulation induction, and inadvertent exposure
novedades.fuentes: Facchinetti F, et al. Reduction of oocyte quality and clinical outcomes using myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol: an update, Expert Opin Drug Metab Toxicol (2020) · Unfer V, et al. Myo-inositol effects in women with PCOS: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Endocr Connect (2017) · Cochrane: Inositol for subfertility associated with PCOS (Review, 2023 update) · ESHRE/ASRM/Monash PCOS Guideline (2023) · Poyatos-León R, et al. The effect of myo-inositol supplementation on gestational diabetes mellitus prevention: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2026;235(5):1024-1036. DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2026.05.020 · Motuhifonua SK, et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023;CD011507.pub3
novedades.texto: Mechanism: myo-inositol and D-chiro-inositol are second messengers in the insulin signaling pathway — supplementation improves ovarian insulin sensitivity, reduces compensatory hyperinsulinemia, and thereby favors resumption of ovulatory cycles in PMOS. It is not a drug in the strict sense but a dietary nutrient/supplement, which shapes its reproductive safety profile (see the inadvertent exposure note below). Indication: ovulatory dysfunction in PMOS/metabolic phenotype, as an adjunct or alternative to metformin in patients with digestive intolerance to the latter; also used as an adjuvant in ovulation induction/IVF protocols to improve oocyte quality. Dose: the 2023 international PCOS guideline (Teede et al., practice point 4.7.4) states that specific types, doses or combinations of inositol cannot be recommended for lack of evidence, and considers it experimental in infertility (5.8.1). Trials often used 2-4 g/day of myo-inositol, sometimes with D-chiro-inositol 40:1, but that regimen comes from studies, not a guideline-recommended dose. If prescribed, agree on it with the patient according to her preferences and reassess at 3-6 months. Evidence: the Cochrane review (2023 update) on inositol for PMOS-associated subfertility finds low-to-moderate certainty evidence favoring a possible improvement in clinical pregnancy and ovulation rates versus placebo, with meta-analyses by Unfer et al. and Facchinetti et al. also showing benefit on metabolic parameters (HOMA-IR, androgen profile) — overall evidence quality remains limited by study size and heterogeneity. Inadvertent exposure during fertility recovery (relevant in women coming off tirzepatide/semaglutide who are improving their metabolic profile): as a physiological nutrient normally present in the diet rather than a synthetic molecule with dedicated teratogenicity studies, myo-inositol is not subject to the same preconception washout restrictions as GLP-1/GIP analogues — no teratogenic warning signal has been described with continued use during an unrecognized pregnancy, and it has in fact also been studied as a supplement for gestational diabetes prevention in at-risk populations. This does not exempt confirming the pregnancy and reassessing the overall therapeutic plan as soon as it is detected. Specific meta-analysis on myo-inositol and gestational diabetes prevention (Poyatos-León R, et al. Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2026;235(5):1024-1036. DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2026.05.020): 12 randomized controlled trials, 4,765 women without preexisting diabetes (pregnant or planning conception within 6 months), search through April 2025. Myo-inositol supplementation substantially reduced the risk of gestational diabetes versus control (44% relative risk reduction), with no significant differences in hypertensive disorders, cesarean delivery, macrosomia, preterm birth, or neonatal hypoglycemia. Cochrane review on prevention of gestational diabetes (Motuhifonua et al. 2023, CD011507.pub3): 7 RCTs with 1,319 women overall; gestational diabetes in 6 RCTs with 1,140 (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.31-0.90; very low certainty); hypertensive disorders in 5 RCTs with 1,052 (RR 0.34; 95% CI 0.19-0.61; low certainty). ⚠️ Cochrane shows a reduction in hypertensive disorders and Poyatos-León finds no difference: the hypertensive finding is not conclusive.

novedades.fuentes: National Library of Medicine. Metformin/Semaglutide/Tirzepatide. Drugs and Lactation Database (LactMed®) · Diab H, Fuquay T, Datta P, Bickel U, Thompson J, Krutsch K. Subcutaneous Semaglutide during Breastfeeding: Infant Safety Regarding Drug Transfer into Human Milk. Nutrients. 2024;16(17):2886 · ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) injection — Prescribing Information, DailyMed, section 8.2 Lactation · AAP (metformin compatibility with breastfeeding)
novedades.texto: Metformin: compatible with breastfeeding — infant exposure via milk is generally <0.5% of the weight-adjusted maternal dose, with no adverse effects reported (LactMed, updated 15 August 2026; greater caution in newborns, preterm infants, and infants with renal impairment). LactMed also lists a postpartum restart schedule of 500 mg every 12 hours from day one — useful if an immediate postpartum restart is chosen. Semaglutide: in the only dedicated study to date (Diab et al., Nutrients 2024; 8 women, SC doses 0.25-1 mg/week), semaglutide was not detectable in any of the milk samples analyzed after subcutaneous administration. The authors themselves note the data remain limited — long-term follow-up and data on maternal nutrition/milk composition are lacking. LactMed: use only injectable semaglutide during breastfeeding; some oral forms contain salcaprozate sodium, which may enter milk and accumulate in the infant. Tirzepatide: per the Zepbound label (DailyMed, section 8.2), in 11 breastfeeding women after a single 5 mg SC dose, tirzepatide was undetectable in 164 of 171 milk samples; the cumulative amount in the remaining 7 samples represented <0.02% of the administered maternal dose — a reassuring figure, though it comes from a single dose, not continuous use over time. The UK Mounjaro label concludes that tirzepatide "could be considered" during breastfeeding; LactMed advises more caution with newborns and preterm infants. With this data it is no longer accurate to say "dedicated studies are lacking" for semaglutide/tirzepatide in lactation — they do exist, although small and short-term. Still distinguish the real risk of infant exposure (low, per this preliminary data) from the mere convenience of restarting maternal treatment as soon as possible — two distinct considerations that should not be blended when counseling the patient.

novedades.fuentes: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. WEGOVY (semaglutide) prescribing information. Revised 2026 · European Medicines Agency. Mounjaro (tirzepatide). Summary of Product Characteristics · Eli Lilly and Company. Mounjaro (tirzepatide) SmPC · U.S. Food and Drug Administration. ZEPBOUND (tirzepatide) prescribing information · Imbroane M, LeMoine K, Nau C, et al. AJOG 2025;233(2):116.e1-e7 · European Medicines Agency. Bydureon (exenatide) SmPC · U.S. Food and Drug Administration. SAXENDA (liraglutide) prescribing information, 2026
novedades.texto: Semaglutide: the 2026 FDA Wegovy label recommends stopping ≥2 months before trying to conceive, due to its prolonged half-life (~1 week, ~5 half-lives for near-complete elimination). This applies to all its presentations (injectable, including the 7.2 mg dose, and tablets). Tirzepatide: here the regulatory agencies differ, and CaVeSal presents both positions without resolving them, so you can decide according to the patient's context: the European label (EMA/Lilly Mounjaro SmPC) recommends stopping ≥1 month before trying to conceive (UK/European label revised 29/08/2026); the U.S. prescribing information (FDA, Zepbound) does not set a mandatory preconception window and instead instructs discontinuing upon recognizing pregnancy — reflecting a genuine difference in regulatory stance, not an error in either source. Tirzepatide elimination half-life: about 5-6 days (FDA label). Liraglutide (daily dosing, half-life about 13 hours): the FDA Saxenda label sets no preconception interval; it instructs stopping when pregnancy is recognized. There is no validated interval; do not use a fixed figure. Extended-release exenatide (weekly): the European Bydureon label (EMA) states it should not be used in pregnancy and should be stopped at least 3 months before a planned pregnancy. Dulaglutide, short-acting exenatide, lixisenatide: the labels of these molecules do not set a specific preconception washout window the way semaglutide/tirzepatide do — the usual instruction is to discontinue upon confirming pregnancy, with no preconception interval validated by dedicated studies. ⚠️ Absence of a validated interval does not mean "no need to stop before trying to conceive" — in the absence of specific data, a prudent approach is to apply a criterion similar to semaglutide (weekly-order half-lives) for dulaglutide (weekly depot); for short-acting exenatide and lixisenatide (daily dosing) there are no specific data. Retatrutide: a triple GLP-1/GIP/glucagon agonist still under investigation — not approved for general clinical use as of this guide (see the Incretin development pipeline guide). It therefore has no indication or label for use in a population seeking pregnancy; any exposure would occur in the context of a clinical trial, with its own study-specific contraception/washout protocol — do not extrapolate the windows above to this molecule. Imbroane et al. (AJOG 2025;233(2):116.e1-e7; n=4,267 per cohort after matching, 8,534 total) found, in their retrospective preconception cohort (TriNetX), an association with lower incidence of gestational diabetes (18.2% vs. 15.2%; OR 0.81; 95% CI 0.72-0.91), hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (22.8% vs. 19.9%; OR 0.84; 95% CI 0.76-0.94), preterm delivery (4.4% vs. 3.0%; OR 0.68; 95% CI 0.54-0.85), and cesarean delivery (19.7% vs. 17.6%; OR 0.89; 95% CI 0.87-0.97) in the group with prior GLP-1/GIP prescription versus the unexposed group. ⚠️ Before matching, the exposed group had a much higher prevalence of overweight/obesity (76.8% vs. 10.7%), type 2 diabetes (37.6% vs. 1.5%), hypertension (32.5% vs. 3.7%), and prior GDM (25.3% vs. 10.0%) — matching adjusted only for age/race/ethnicity/comorbidity categories, not finely for these factors, so much of this apparent protection may reflect residual confounding by indication (who receives GLP-1/GIP) rather than a true protective drug effect. This does not change this guide's preconception washout recommendation — see also the Inadvertent pregnancy during GLP-1/tirzepatide guide for a contrasting read on maternal metabolic/hypertensive outcomes.

novedades.titulo: MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy
novedades.fuentes: NAMS Position Statement (2022) · Heinemann et al. (2004) · Manual para Manejo de la Mujer en Edad del Climaterio, 2nd ed. (SOCHEG, 2020) · Stute P, et al. EMAS 2026 framework, Maturitas 2026;212:109060 · MSPyBS Paraguay Res. S.G. No. 267/2023 · ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13. Management of Menopause-Related Vasomotor, Sleep, and Mood Symptoms. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;148(5):e345-e364 · Qaseem A, et al. ACP. Ann Intern Med 2026. doi:10.7326/ANNALS-26-01205
novedades.texto: MRS (11 items): somatic, psychological, urogenital. NAMS/Heinemann scheme (total score only): 0-4 none or little · 5-8 mild · 9-15 moderate · ≥16 severe (consider HRT). SOCHEG scheme (broken down by domain, each with its own severe-alteration cutoff): Somatic (items 1-4) ≥8 · Psychological (items 5-8) ≥6 · Urogenital (items 9-11) ≥3 · Total (items 1-11) ≥15. HRT by uterine status: no uterus → estrogen alone. Uterus present, perimenopause → sequential/cyclic. Postmenopause → continuous combined. Transdermal HRT (preferred, especially with hypertension, obesity BMI>30, hypertriglyceridemia, VTE risk): 17β-Estradiol gel 0.75-1.25g/day, or patches 25-50mcg/day. Endometrial protection (intact uterus): Micronized natural progesterone 200mg/day for 10-14 days/month (sequential regimen) or 100mg/day continuous · or Dydrogesterone 10-20mg/day. Tibolone (STEAR): 2.5mg/day PO (or 1.25mg/day in lower body weight or advanced perimenopause) — covers vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and bone loss prevention (estrogen doses to prevent bone loss and what to do when MHT is stopped: see Osteoporosis and bone densitometry); does not require an added progestogen. Tissue-selective estrogen complex (alternative when avoiding a progestogen is preferred): Conjugated equine estrogens 0.45mg/day + Bazedoxifene 20mg/day — bazedoxifene (a SERM) replaces the progestogen for endometrial protection, without the bleeding or breast tenderness associated with it. Evidence from the SMART-1/SMART-2 trials (12 weeks): significant reduction in hot flush frequency/severity vs. placebo, with a 50% reduction by day 8-10 and a sustained ~90% reduction by day 83 of use; no increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, VTE, stroke or coronary disease in pooled analyses (follow-up up to 2 years — confidence limited by low event incidence and lack of longer-term data). ⚠️ Availability in Paraguay not confirmed — verify locally before prescribing. Alternative endometrial protection — 52mg LNG-IUD: off-label use alongside systemic estrogen to provide endometrial protection (plus contraception if applicable) — replace at 5 years when used for this purpose (the approved contraceptive lifespan is 8 years, but the evidence supporting endometrial protection in HRT covers up to 5 years). Local availability (Paraguay, confirm against the current pharmacy/distributor): transdermal 17β-estradiol gel/spray (e.g., Ginoderm) — available. 17β-estradiol vaginal ring — not available. Conjugated equine estrogens + bazedoxifene — availability unconfirmed. This information is contextual, to anticipate the availability conversation with the patient — it should not be used to exclude an option from the clinical list. Interaction with GLP-1/GIP agonists: the gastric emptying delay induced by semaglutide/tirzepatide (more pronounced with the latter) may reduce absorption of oral HRT — in patients on GLP-1/GIP therapy, prefer the transdermal route for estrogen therapy (same pharmacokinetic principle as in the Contraception during tirzepatide guide). Order of pharmacologic treatment for vasomotor symptoms (ACP 2026): 1st line — estrogen + progestogen with a uterus, or estrogen alone without a uterus (strong recommendation, high certainty). 2nd line, if contraindicated or not tolerated — SNRI: desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine. 3rd line — SSRI (escitalopram or paroxetine), gabapentin or NK antagonists (fezolinetant or elinzanetant): see Fezolinetant and elinzanetant. Shared decision: benefits, harms, comorbidities, preferences, cost and availability.

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Cancellation criteria and OHSS prevention
novedades.fuentes: ESHRE Female Infertility Guideline (2023), Hum Reprod Open 2023(3):hoad034 · ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348
novedades.texto: In low-complexity techniques (timed intercourse/IUI), the safety threshold requires strictly avoiding high-order multiple pregnancy and Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS). Immediate cancellation criteria — do NOT give hCG: ≥3 mature follicles (≥15-16mm) in women <35 years, or >3-4 mature follicles in any low-complexity patient. More than 4-6 intermediate follicles (11-14mm) that could respond to the trigger. Serum estradiol >1,000-1,500pg/mL (if measured). Management on cancellation: cancel and withhold the hCG trigger (it is the direct trigger for the VEGF cascade and capillary hyperpermeability of OHSS). Advise strict coital abstinence or mandatory condom use for ≥7-10 days. Do not give hCG for luteal support. Rescue option at a high-complexity center: convert the cycle to IVF with follicular aspiration, GnRH-agonist trigger, and total embryo cryopreservation ("freeze-all").

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Follicular size for the hCG trigger
novedades.fuentes: ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348 · ASRM Practice Committee (2020), Fertil Steril 113:66-70 · Palatnik et al. (2012), Fertil Steril 97:1089-1094 · Shalom-Paz et al. (2014), Gynecol Endocrinol 30(2):107-110 · Ling et al. (2024), Eur J Med Res 29:184 · Van Oirschot et al. (2025), Fertil Steril · ESHRE Ovarian Stimulation Guideline (2025) · ESHRE Female Infertility Guideline (2023), Hum Reprod Open 2023(3):hoad034
novedades.texto: The hCG trigger mimics the endogenous LH surge: it resumes oocyte meiosis, luteinizes the granulosa cells, and times follicular rupture (36-40h after administration). Trigger agents: Recombinant hCG (r-hCG) 250mcg SC · urinary hCG (u-hCG) 5,000-10,000 IU IM. Follicular size by inducing agent: Clomiphene citrate: trigger with the leading follicle at a mean diameter of 20-28mm; ASRM notes higher pregnancy rates at 23-28mm (follicles under clomiphene mature at larger diameters: in conception cycles the leading follicle measured 20.4 ± 1.2mm). Monitor endometrial thickness because of the antiestrogenic effect. Letrozole: trigger with the leading follicle at 19-23mm (optimal 19.1-21mm in the first IUI cycle); tolerated up to 28mm. Gonadotropins (FSH/hMG): trigger with the leading follicle at 16-18mm (oocyte maturity is reached at slightly smaller sizes under direct gonadotropins; triggering above 19-20mm increases oocyte senescence). Note: ESHRE (2025) considers that the association between follicle size and outcome has not been sufficiently studied; the trigger size is individualized. Concurrent endometrial status: ideally ≥7mm with a trilaminar pattern before ordering the trigger. Timing of intercourse/insemination: timed intercourse — the night of the trigger and again 36h later (or on alternating days: trigger day and the next). IUI — sperm preparation and insemination at 36h (range 34-38h) post-hCG.

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Therapeutic choice: Letrozole vs. Clomiphene vs. Gonadotropins
novedades.fuentes: ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348 · Teede et al., Int'l PCOS Guideline (2023), Fertil Steril 120(4):767-793 · ESHRE Female Infertility Guideline (2023), Hum Reprod Open 2023(3):hoad034 · MSPyBS Paraguay (2025), Res. S.G. Nº 050/2025
novedades.texto: Letrozole (aromatase inhibitor) — first-line in PCOS/WHO Type II anovulation, especially with overweight/obesity (BMI≥25-30). Higher cumulative ovulation, clinical pregnancy and live-birth rates than clomiphene (PPCOS II trial). Does not block endometrial or cervical estrogen receptors (preserves endometrial thickness and cervical mucus quality). Short half-life (~48h): favors monofollicular development, lower multiple-pregnancy rate. Clomiphene citrate (SERM): first-line alternative when letrozole is unavailable/not tolerated, or in unexplained infertility (timed intercourse/IUI). Drawback: prolonged peripheral antiestrogenic effect (half-life >2 weeks) — refractory thin endometrium (<7mm) and hostile mucus; higher multifollicular/multiple-pregnancy rate (5-10%, mostly twins) than letrozole. Exogenous gonadotropins (recombinant FSH / hMG): failure or resistance to oral agents (after 3-6 ovulatory cycles without conception); or Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (WHO Type I — hypothalamic-pituitary axis not intact, clomiphene/letrozole do NOT work, requires hMG or FSH+hCG/LH microdose); or as an adjunct in low-complexity/IUI cycles.

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Dosing regimens and stimulation protocols
novedades.fuentes: ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348 · ESHRE Female Infertility Guideline (2023), Hum Reprod Open 2023(3):hoad034 · MSPyBS Paraguay (2025), Res. S.G. Nº 050/2025
novedades.texto: Letrozole: 2.5mg/day PO x5 days, starting cycle day 2-5. If no ovulation, escalate to 5.0mg/day the next cycle; maximum dose 7.5mg/day x5 days. Clomiphene citrate: 50mg/day PO x5 days, day 2-5. If no response, increase to 100mg/day; usual maximum 150mg/day x5 days (higher doses do not improve pregnancy rates and worsen the endometrial antiestrogenic effect). Limit: 6 ovulatory cycles. Gonadotropins — "Low-Dose Step-Up" protocol: strict goal of monofollicular development and OHSS prevention. Starting dose 37.5-50-75 IU/day SC/IM from cycle day 2-3, holding the fixed dose for 7-14 days. If after 14 days there is no follicular selection (no follicle ≥10mm), increase 50% weekly (e.g. 37.5→75 IU/day) until a response is seen, then maintain that dose through the trigger.

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Treatment failure and drug resistance
novedades.fuentes: ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348
novedades.texto: Drug resistance: persistent absence of recruitment, or no follicles ≥15mm despite maximum doses. Clomiphene resistance: anovulation after 150mg/day x5 days. Letrozole resistance: anovulation after 7.5mg/day x5 days. Management: switch therapeutic line (CC→Letrozole, add Metformin in PCOS with insulin resistance, or move to low-dose gonadotropins). Failed induction (treatment failure): confirmed regular ovulatory cycles (optimal follicular development, follicular rupture and adequate luteal phase with progesterone ≥10ng/mL) without pregnancy after 4-6 consecutive ovulatory cycles. Management: full couple re-evaluation (tubal patency by HSG if not yet done, repeat semen analysis with TMSC) and escalation to high-complexity ART (IVF/ICSI). Endometrial failure (antiestrogenic effect): adequate follicular growth but persistently thin endometrium (<6-7mm) in the preovulatory window (common with clomiphene). Management: switch to letrozole or add exogenous estrogen support.

novedades.titulo: Ovulation induction — Baseline and serial ultrasound monitoring
novedades.fuentes: ASRM Practice Committee (2013), Fertil Steril 100:341-348 · ESHRE Female Infertility Guideline (2023), Hum Reprod Open 2023(3):hoad034
novedades.texto: Baseline transvaginal ultrasound + Antral Follicle Count (AFC), cycle days 2-4 — mandatory before starting any inducing agent: thin, shed endometrium (<5mm); rule out functional cysts/persistent follicles from the previous cycle (start if no follicles/cysts >10mm; postpone/cancel if a residual cyst or growing follicle ≥10-15mm is found, usually with baseline E2 >50-60pg/mL). AFC (bilateral 2-9mm follicles): <5-7 suggests low ovarian reserve · 8-15 normal reserve · ≥20 (or ovarian volume ≥10mL) polycystic ovarian morphology — maximum alert for hyperresponse and OHSS risk. Serial follow-up: first post-stimulation scan on cycle day 8-10, then every 48-72h depending on follicular growth rate (expected physiologic growth 1.5-2mm/day). Record the mean diameter in 2 perpendicular planes per ovary, and endometrial thickness/pattern (optimal: periovulatory trilaminar "triple line" ≥7-8mm).

novedades.fuentes: Own table CaVeSal® · Based on: Cicero S et al. (nasal bone) · Kagan KO et al. (TR and DV) · FMF/Nicolaides
novedades.texto: Finding Interpretation and management Absent nasal bone Absent in ~60–70% of T21. In euploid fetuses: 2.2% in Caucasian, 5% in Asian and 9% in Afro-Caribbean women; falls with CRL (4.7% at 45–54 mm, 1% at 75–84 mm) and rises with NT (Cicero 2004). Integrate with NT and other markers. Ductus venosus with absent or reversed a-wave Marker of aneuploidy and congenital heart disease. Refer to Fetal Medicine, echocardiography. Tricuspid regurgitation Associated with T21 and congenital heart disease. Fetal echocardiography. Choroid plexus cyst(s) Soft marker, more associated with T18 than T21. Isolated with normal screening: low residual risk. 2 or more abnormal findings Increased chromosomal risk: refer to Fetal Medicine for genetic counselling; NIPT or invasive testing (CVS 11–13+6 wk) according to informed choice.

novedades.titulo: Intrahepatic cholestasis: MSPBS criterion and references
novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® table · Based on: MSPBS/SPGO 2018 (national criterion) · MINSAL Chile 2015 Perinatal Guide · RCOG GTG 43 (2022)
novedades.texto: MSPBS 2018 Criterion Management Low risk Bile acids 10–19 µmol/L with normal enzymes Outpatient, weekly tests; elective delivery at 36–37 wk Moderate risk Bile acids 20–39 and/or AST/ALT raised up to twice normal ≥28 wk: admission, tests every 72 h; if no response, manage as high risk. Delivery 36–37 wk (CaVeSal® suggestion: the manual sets no week for this group) High risk Bile acids ≥40 and/or enzymes >2× and/or no response to treatment Always admit. <34 wk: UDCA at maximum dose; if no improvement, lung maturation and delivery. ≥36 wk: deliver National criterion (Paraguay): Manual Nacional de Normas de Atención de las Principales Patologías Obstétricas (MSPBS/SPGO 2018), ch. 5. Diagnosis: itching + bile acids ≥10 µmol/L and/or raised enzymes or bilirubin. UDCA 10–16 mg/kg/day in 2 doses (start 900 mg/day, maximum 1200 mg/day). Follow-up: liver profile, bile acids and PT every 1–2 wk; CTG every 3–7 days. Regional reference (MINSAL Chile 2015): anicteric 38 wk; icteric (bilirubin >1.2 + raised enzymes) 36 wk. International reference (RCOG GTG 43, 2022): diagnosis ≥19 µmol/L; 19–39 birth by 40 wk; 40–99 38–39 wk; ≥100 35–36 wk. With ≥100, consider earlier delivery. In all cases: deliver if fetal wellbeing is compromised, regardless of GA.

novedades.titulo: Management when the entered data are normal
novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® suggestion · Based on: ESHRE 2022 · FIGO · MSPBS Paraguay · SMFM Consult Series #74 (2025) · ACOG Practice Advisory (2026) · ACOG CO 797 (2020) · CDC/ACIP · ISUOG · WHO (calcium) · Dwarkanath P et al. NEJM 2024
novedades.texto: Calculate button: every entered item returns a result and a management step, also when normal. If a test is already entered its result is used; if it is missing and needed, it is suggested. Labs within range: summary of the normal values. Repeat according to the Lab schedule. Fasting glucose <92 mg/dL before 24 wk: 75 g OGTT at 24–28 wk. Non-reactive serologies (HIV, syphilis, HBsAg, hepatitis C, Chagas): repeat according to the Lab schedule. Anti-HBs negative: not immune to hepatitis B; the vaccine is safe in pregnancy, give it if HBsAg is negative. CMV IgG negative: susceptible; hygiene measures (hand washing after changing diapers, do not share utensils with young children). Group B streptococcus negative: no intrapartum prophylaxis; the result is valid for 5 weeks. Recurrent pregnancy loss (2 or more miscarriages): antiphospholipid work-up (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2 glycoprotein I), TSH and anti-TPO, early follow-up. Grand multiparity (5 or more births/caesareans): higher risk of postpartum haemorrhage and malpresentation; birth plan with active management of the third stage. 2 or more caesareans: planned repeat caesarean per MSPBS Paraguay; if she arrives in the second stage, manage as one previous caesarean. Normal 1st-trimester screening: scan without markers, low combined risk or low-risk cell-free DNA: anomaly scan at 20–22 wk. Age ≥35 with scan only: offer cell-free DNA or combined test. If screening is already entered, the age card does not request it again. Anomaly scan without anomalies: 3rd-trimester growth according to overall risk; suggests cervical length and 2T uterine PI if not recorded. Fetal weight: P10–P89, appropriate growth. P3–P10 without Doppler: request Doppler (UA, MCA/CPR, uterine) to distinguish SGA from FGR. Supplementation: prophylactic iron 30–60 mg/day with normal Hb (WHO); with MTHFR, standard folic acid (methylfolate optional); vitamin D according to the entered value; calcium at the physician's discretion (WHO in low intake vs. Cochrane 2025 no effect on pre-eclampsia); see Supplementation in pregnancy.

novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® own table · Based on: WHO (iron and folic acid; calcium) · CDC · IOM 2011 · Cluver CA et al. Cochrane 2025 · Dwarkanath P et al. NEJM 2024 · ATA 2017 · Middleton P et al. Cochrane 2018
novedades.texto: Folic acid: 0.4–0.8 mg/day from preconception to at least 12 wk. High dose with a previous NTD (previous pregnancy, or the woman or her partner with an NTD), epilepsy or antiseizure drugs, obesity or diabetes: 4 mg/day (ACOG PB 187, CDC) or 5 mg/day (NICE, RCOG), from 3 months before conception to 12 wk; then return to the standard dose. Another previous malformation does not justify it. In Obstetric history, the “Previous NTD” box activates the high dose. MTHFR: folic acid remains the standard (CDC), as it is the only form proven to prevent NTDs. Methylfolate (5-MTHF) 400–800 µg/day is an optional alternative. Iron: prophylaxis 30–60 mg/day elemental iron (WHO). Anaemia: 120 mg/day until Hb normalises, then back to prophylaxis. Hb <7 g/dL: IV iron from the 2nd trimester and consider transfusion according to the clinical picture. Calcium: requirement 1000 mg/day (1300 under 19 years), the same as outside pregnancy. WHO: 1.5–2 g/day in 3 doses in low-intake populations. Cochrane 2025 (10 trials, 37,504 women): no difference in pre-eclampsia in the large trials. Physician's decision; separate from iron. Iodine: 150 µg/day supplement (potassium iodide) from preconception; total intake target 250 µg/day. Avoid supplements >500 µg/day and seaweed. Omega-3: with risk of preterm birth, 500–1000 mg/day DHA+EPA before 20 wk (Cochrane 2018: 42% fewer births <34 wk). Effect on pre-eclampsia uncertain. Vitamin D: see the vitamin D section in this tab.

novedades.fuentes: Table adapted (translated) from Alexander EK et al. ATA 2017 · CaVeSal® suggestion · Based on: ATA 2011 · Endocrine Society 2012 · ETA 2014 · Lazarus JH et al. NEJM 2012 · Casey BM et al. NEJM 2017
novedades.texto: Use the laboratory pregnancy range. If not reported: TSH upper limit 4.0 µIU/mL (ATA 2017; the trimester no longer changes the cutoff). Check anti-TPO if TSH is >2.5 in the 1st trimester (ATA 2017, rec. 28) or >3.0 in the 2nd–3rd (CaVeSal® suggestion). Anti-TPO TSH (µIU/mL) Levothyroxine Anti-TPO+ >4.0 (above range) Recommended Anti-TPO+ 2.5–4.0 Consider Anti-TPO− ≥10 Recommended Anti-TPO− 4.0–10 Consider Anti-TPO− <4.0 Do not treat Grey zone (CaVeSal® suggestion): TSH >2.5 in T1 or >3.0 in T2–T3 and ≤4.0: check anti-TPO; if positive, consider levothyroxine. History of the cutoffs: ATA 2011 and Endocrine Society 2012: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.0 by trimester. ETA 2014: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5. ATA 2017 replaced them with the laboratory range or 4.0. Trials: CATS (Lazarus 2012, 21,846 women, treatment at ~13 weeks: IQ at 3 years 99.2 vs 100.0) and Casey (2017, TSH ≥4.0, treatment at ~17 weeks: IQ at 5 years 97 vs 94) showed no neurodevelopmental benefit. The link between high TSH and cognitive deficit is observational. Preconception: treated hypothyroid women, TSH between the lower limit and 2.5. IVF/ICSI with subclinical hypothyroidism: levothyroxine with a TSH goal <2.5 (ATA 2017, rec. 20). Low TSH in T1: may be physiological due to hCG; confirm with free T4 and, if Graves disease is suspected, TRAb. Low free T4 with normal TSH: isolated hypothyroxinemia; not routinely treated. Free T4 varies by method and trimester.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Grobman WA et al. (NICHD) 2007 · MSPBS Paraguay · FIGO 2025 · ACOG · RCOG · RANZCOG
novedades.texto: Candidate: one previous caesarean with a low transverse scar. Favour success: previous vaginal birth and non-recurrent previous indication. Assess carefully: potentially recurrent previous indication; previous uterine surgery according to myometrial extent. Absolute contraindication: classical or inverted-T scar. Two or more caesareans: planned repeat caesarean per MSPBS Paraguay (vaginal birth is discouraged; uterine rupture ~1.4 %). If she arrives in the second stage: manage as one previous caesarean. International view: ACOG, RCOG and RANZCOG allow vaginal birth after 2 caesareans with senior obstetrician counselling; FIGO is more restrictive. With 3 or more, evidence is very limited. The Calculator estimates the probability of success with the Grobman score. Requirements: immediate surgical availability and informed consent; discuss the risk of uterine rupture (0.5–0.9 %). Misoprostol is contraindicated.

novedades.texto: Clinical presentation: predominantly nocturnal itching of the palms and soles, in the 2nd-3rd trimester, with no primary skin lesions. Pruritus may precede laboratory abnormalities by days. Laboratory cutoffs used by the CaVeSal prenatal calculator Parameter Normal Abnormal Meaning AST/ALT <40 IU/L >40 IU/L (>70 IU/L: suspect HELLP) Elevated enzymes = criterion for ICP LDH — >400 moderate · >600 IU/L >600 suggests hemolysis/HELLP, not ICP Total bilirubin ≤1.2 mg/dL >1.2 mg/dL Defines the icteric form Alkaline phosphatase — >300 moderate · >500 IU/L high Poorly specific (placental origin) Total bile acids (TBA) <10 µmol/L 10–19 low · 20–39 moderate · ≥40 high (MSPBS 2018) Specific marker; optional (not available at many centers) National criterion — MSPBS/SPGO 2018, ch. 5 (CaVeSal prenatal calculator) Risk Criterion Management Low Bile acids 10–19 µmol/L · normal enzymes Outpatient, weekly control · elective delivery 36–37 wk Moderate Bile acids 20–39 and/or AST/ALT up to 2× ≥28 wk: admission, control every 72 h · if no response, high risk · delivery 36–37 wk* High Bile acids ≥40 and/or enzymes >2× (>80 IU/L) and/or no response Always admit · <34 wk without improvement on maximum-dose UDCA: lung maturation and delivery · ≥36 wk: deliver *CaVeSal® suggestion: the manual sets no week for moderate risk. Regional reference (MINSAL Chile 2015): anicteric → 38 wk · icteric (bilirubin >1.2 + enzymes) → 36 wk. In all cases: UDCA 10–16 mg/kg/day in 2 doses (start 900 mg/day, maximum 1200 mg/day) + oral vitamin K if cholestasis is prolonged. Follow-up: liver profile, bile acids and PT every 1–2 wk; CTG every 3–7 days. Deliver if fetal well-being is compromised, regardless of gestational age. novedades.texto: FIGO 2019 clinical classification Grade Intraoperative finding 1 Adherent placenta (creta): no myometrial invasion 2 Increta: myometrial invasion, without reaching the serosa 3a Percreta limited to the uterine serosa 3b Percreta with bladder invasion 3c Percreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues or organs Risk of placenta accreta spectrum with placenta previa according to number of cesarean deliveries (Silver 2006) Cesarean delivery 1ª 2ª 3ª 4ª ≥5ª Risk of PAS 3% 11% 40% 61% 67% Without placenta previa, risk ranges from 0.24% to 6.74% according to the number of cesarean deliveries. Ultrasound signs (ISUOG 2016): loss of the retroplacental clear zone, placental lacunae, myometrial thinning <1 mm, disruption of the bladder line, placental bulge, focal exophytic mass; Doppler: uterovesical or subplacental hypervascularity and bridging vessels. Antenatal diagnosis (WAPM/PMF 2026): after a previous cesarean, early transvaginal ultrasound to rule out cesarean scar pregnancy (a potential precursor of PAS); in the 2nd-3rd trimester, combined transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound; MRI is only complementary (inconclusive ultrasound, non-anterior or non-previa placenta). If suspected, refer to a perinatal center with a multidisciplinary team. novedades.texto: Group Management Sources 1 Prolonged latent phase and slow but progressive labor are not indications for cesarean. Partograph according to the chosen model (Ministry CLAP from 4 cm, WHO 2020 from 5 cm, ACOG from 6 cm). Active-phase arrest: ≥6 cm with ruptured membranes and no change with ≥4 h of adequate contractions or ≥6 h of oxytocin with inadequate contractions. Second stage: ≥3 h of pushing before diagnosing arrest (longer with epidural, individualized). Continuous support. WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 2a / 4a Induce only with a clear indication; from 41+0 weeks induction is recommended. Bishop ≤6: cervical ripening (oral misoprostol 25 µg q2h or vaginal 25 µg q6h, balloon, or balloon + oxytocin). Do not diagnose failed induction in the latent phase before ≥24 h of induction and ≥12-18 h of oxytocin after membrane rupture. Never unsupervised; induce where an operating room is available. WHO — Induction of labour at or beyond term (2022) · WHO — Induction of labour (2011) · WHO — Mechanical methods (2022) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 2b / 4b Verify and document the indication. Without a medical indication, do not schedule before 39 weeks. ACOG CO 765 (2019) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 3 Same criteria as Group 1 with multiparous standards. Second stage: ≥2 h of pushing. Lowest cesarean rate group: a cesarean here deserves review of the indication. WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 5.1 VBAC if: low transverse (or low vertical) incision, no previous rupture and no contraindication to vaginal birth. Contraindicated: classical cesarean, T or J incision, previous rupture. Only with 24-h emergency cesarean, blood bank and NICU. Continuous fetal monitoring and one-to-one care (abnormal FHR is the most common sign of rupture). Induction with mechanical methods; misoprostol contraindicated; oxytocin with caution. Epidural not contraindicated. Interval under 18 months: higher risk. EFW >4500 g: cesarean (FIGO). FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45 · WHO — Induction of labour (2011) 5.2 MSPBS Paraguay: with 2 or more cesareans, planned repeat cesarean from 39 weeks; vaginal birth is discouraged (uterine rupture ~1.4%). If she arrives in the second stage, manage as one previous cesarean. International view: with two cesareans, FIGO generally does not recommend VBAC (only with a previous vaginal birth, senior obstetrician counseling and a high-complexity center); RCOG and ACOG allow it with counseling. Three or more: insufficient data on VBAC (ACOG PB 205); cesarean is usually scheduled. With placenta previa or low anterior placenta, rule out accreta. MSPBS Paraguay — Obstetric conditions · FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45 6 Offer external cephalic version (ECV) from 36 weeks. Without ECV: planned cesarean from 39 weeks, or vaginal breech birth only with an institutional protocol, trained operator and written consent. In labor: ultrasound (type of breech, head flexion, EFW) and continuous monitoring; inadequate progress → cesarean. Imminent delivery: hands-off assistance. ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b 7 Same as Group 6, with ECV from 37 weeks. With one previous low transverse cesarean, ECV may be attempted if she is a good VBAC candidate. ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b · FIGO — VBAC (2025) 8 Uncomplicated dichorionic or monochorionic diamniotic twins, >32 weeks, first twin cephalic, no significant discordance: vaginal birth and cesarean are equally safe. First twin non-cephalic: cesarean. Monoamniotic: cesarean (32+0-33+6). Triplets: cesarean. One previous low transverse cesarean does not contraindicate VBAC. Active third stage due to higher hemorrhage risk. NICE NG137 (2019) · ACOG PB 231 (2021) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) · FIGO — VBAC (2025) 9 In labor or with ruptured membranes: cesarean (cord prolapse, uterine rupture). Before labor and without contraindications: ECV from 37 weeks. Ultrasound to rule out a mechanical cause (placenta previa, fibroids, anomalies). With back down, consider a vertical uterine incision. GLOWM · StatPearls — ECV 10 Lung maturation, neuroprotection, tocolysis and PROM according to the preterm labor and PROM cards in this guide. Notify neonatology. Prematurity alone does not determine the mode of birth; it is decided by obstetric conditions. ACOG CO 831 (2021) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: sources listed for each group · PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification (2018). Fetal lung maturation, magnesium sulfate neuroprotection, tocolysis and PROM follow the management already set in their cards in this guide and in the calculator. Does not replace clinical judgment.

novedades.texto: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS: accreta/increta/percreta). Main risk factor: prior cesarean plus anterior placenta previa/low-lying placenta. ⚠️ Golden rule: whenever signs of accreta are present, never attempt manual placental removal — leave the placenta in situ and proceed to en bloc hysterectomy, at a Level III-IV center, with a planned cesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks. Risk factors: number of prior cesareans, prior uterine curettage, prior uterine surgery (myomectomy), history of Asherman syndrome — in addition to placenta previa/low-lying placenta and maternal age >35 or IVF, already recorded under Morphology and History. 2D ultrasound signs: loss of the clear zone, myometrial thinning (<1mm), irregular placental lacunae ("Swiss cheese" appearance), interruption of the bladder-uterine interface, placental bulging toward the bladder, focal exophytic mass. Color Doppler signs: uterovesical and subplacental hypervascularity, bridging vessels, lacunar feeder vessels, parametrial involvement. FIGO Classification (surgical/histopathological confirmation): Grade 1 (Accreta) · Grade 2 (Increta) · Grade 3a (Percreta limited to the uterine serosa) · Grade 3b (Percreta with urinary bladder invasion) · Grade 3c (Percreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues/organs: broad ligament, vaginal wall, pelvic sidewall or any other pelvic organ, with or without bladder invasion). Jauniaux E, et al. FIGO, Int J Gynecol Obstet 2019;146:20-24. ⚠️ Probability and Extent are calculated using the "CaVeSal Classification" — a proprietary scoring scheme developed by the team (not a published FIGO/ISUOG/ACOG score) that combines risk factors + 2D signs + Doppler signs. The FIGO Classification is a separate data point, based on surgical/histopathological confirmation — it does not replace, and should not be confused with, the CaVeSal Classification. Antenatal diagnosis (WAPM/PMF 2026): cesarean scar pregnancy is a potential precursor of PAS — after a previous cesarean, early transvaginal ultrasound to establish the implantation site. In the 2nd-3rd trimester, combined transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound (placental location, myometrial thickness and contour, uterovesical interface); markers: lacunae, placental bulge, uterovesical hypervascularity and bridging vessels, alone or combined. 2D ultrasound with color Doppler is the mainstay; MRI is complementary (inconclusive ultrasound, non-anterior or non-previa placenta, technical limits). If cesarean scar pregnancy or PAS is suspected: refer to a perinatal center with a multidisciplinary team, blood products, adult and neonatal ICU and complex pelvic surgery; delivery timing is individualized.

novedades.texto: Diagnosis: nocturnal palmoplantar pruritus, without primary skin lesion. Labs: bilirubin, AST/ALT, ALP, GGT. National criterion (MSPBS 2018): Low risk — bile acids 10–19 μmol/L with normal enzymes → outpatient, weekly control, elective delivery at 36–37 wk. Moderate risk — bile acids 20–39 and/or AST/ALT up to 2× → ≥28 wk admission and control every 72 h; if no response, manage as high; delivery at 36–37 wk (CaVeSal® suggestion: the manual sets no week for this group). High risk — bile acids ≥40 and/or enzymes >2× (>80 IU/L) and/or no response → always admit; <34 wk: UDCA up to maximum dose and, if no improvement, lung maturation and delivery; ≥36 wk: deliver. Regional reference (MINSAL Chile 2015): anicteric → 38 wk · icteric (bilirubin >1.2 + enzymes) → 36 wk. International reference (RCOG 2022): diagnosis ≥19 μmol/L · 40–99 → 38–39 wk · ≥100 → 35–36 wk (consider earlier). Treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid 10–16 mg/kg/day in 2 doses (start 900 mg/day, maximum 1200 mg/day) + vitamin K if cholestasis is prolonged. Follow-up: liver profile, bile acids and PT every 1–2 wk; CTG every 3–7 days. ⚠️ Deliver at any sign of fetal compromise, regardless of pathway or GA.

novedades.titulo: Fezolinetant and elinzanetant — NK receptor antagonists, non-hormonal therapy for vasomotor symptoms
novedades.fuentes: Pratt MC, et al. Expert Rev Clin Pharmacol 2023;16(5):389-398 · Panay N, et al. Climacteric 2024;27(3):221-235 · ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;148(5):e345-e364 (Table 2) · Qaseem A, et al. ACP. Ann Intern Med 2026. doi:10.7326/ANNALS-26-01205
novedades.texto: Mechanism: neurokinin receptor antagonists that act on hypothalamic KNDy neurons involved in thermoregulation, with no hormonal action. Fezolinetant: selective NK3 antagonist. Elinzanetant: dual NK1/NK3 antagonist. Fezolinetant: 45mg PO once daily, with or without food. FDA-approved for vasomotor symptoms (VMS). ⚠️ FDA boxed warning: requires baseline liver function testing, repeated monthly during the first 3 months of use, and again at 6 and 9 months. Elinzanetant: 120mg PO once daily. FDA-approved for VMS and also for menopause-related sleep disturbance (a sleep benefit not included in fezolinetant's specific approval). Requires liver function testing before starting and again at 3 months of treatment — a less intensive monitoring cadence than fezolinetant. Indication (both): moderate-to-severe VMS of the climacteric, a non-hormonal alternative when HRT is contraindicated or not the patient's preference (hormone-dependent cancer history, VTE, personal preference). In indirect network comparisons (ACOG CPG13), both drugs show similar efficacy on VMS frequency and severity; elinzanetant showed a greater effect on sleep disturbance (PROMIS sleep disturbance score) in indirect comparison with fezolinetant. Most common adverse effects vs. placebo in the OASIS trials with elinzanetant: headache and fatigue. Place in treatment (ACP 2026): 3rd line (moderate certainty), after HRT and SNRIs (desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine), alongside SSRIs and gabapentin. See MRS Scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy.

novedades.texto: TSH in pregnancy (ATA 2017): use the laboratory pregnancy range. If not reported, upper limit 4.0 µIU/mL; the trimester no longer changes the cutoff. Check anti-TPO if TSH is >2.5 in 1T (ATA 2017, rec. 28) or >3.0 in 2T–3T (CaVeSal® suggestion). Anti-TPO TSH (µIU/mL) Levothyroxine Positive >4.0 (above range) Recommended Positive 2.5–4.0 Consider Negative ≥10 Recommended Negative 4.0–10 Consider Negative <4.0 Do not treat Grey zone (CaVeSal® suggestion): TSH >2.5 in T1 or >3.0 in T2–T3 and ≤4.0: check anti-TPO; if positive, consider levothyroxine. The 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.0 trimester cutoffs came from ATA 2011 and Endocrine Society 2012 (ETA 2014: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5); ATA 2017 replaced them. Trials: CATS (Lazarus 2012; 21,846 women, treatment at ~13 weeks, IQ at 3 years 99.2 vs 100.0) and Casey (2017; TSH ≥4.0, treatment at ~17 weeks, IQ at 5 years 97 vs 94) showed no neurodevelopmental benefit. The link between high TSH and cognitive deficit is observational. Treated hypothyroidism: TSH in the lower half of the range; <2.5 is a reasonable goal. Isolated hypothyroxinemia (low free T4 with normal TSH): not routinely treated. Hyperthyroidism: PTU in T1, methimazole in T2–T3. Never radioactive iodine. In T1 a low TSH may be physiological due to hCG.

Preventing menopause-related bone loss. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025;392:239-248 · The Menopause Society (2021, 2022) · USPSTF (2022) · Ferrari S, et al. SVGO 2026. Swiss Med Wkly 2026;156:5700
novedades.texto: T-Score: normal ≥-1.0 · osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5 · osteoporosis ≤-2.5 · severe +fracture. Z-Score (premenopausal): ≤-2.0 abnormal. FRAX (osteopenia, established postmenopause): treat if major fracture risk ≥20% or hip ≥3%. FRAX and OST are not useful to identify perimenopausal women who will develop osteoporosis. Basic support (all patients): Elemental calcium 1,000-1,500mg/day + Vitamin D3 800-2,000 IU/day (target ≥30ng/mL). Antiresorptives: Alendronate 70mg PO weekly · Risedronate 35mg weekly or 150mg monthly · Zoledronic acid 5mg IV annually · Denosumab 60mg SC every 6 months (do not stop abruptly without transitioning to another antiresorptive, due to rebound vertebral fracture risk). Anabolics (severe osteoporosis/high fracture risk): Teriparatide 20mcg/day SC, maximum 24 months of use. Treatment by risk category (SVGO 2026, Swiss guideline): imminent or very high risk → anabolic first, then antiresorptive consolidation; romosozumab or abaloparatide when the fastest BMD gain is needed, especially at the hip. High risk → bisphosphonates or denosumab first line. Moderate risk → lifestyle + raloxifene or oral bisphosphonate; in selected osteopenia or early osteoporosis, infrequent zoledronate as prevention. Treat-to-target by hip BMD, reassess at 2 years. Check local availability of romosozumab and abaloparatide. Prevention of bone loss in perimenopause and menopause Prevention ≠ treatment: treatment is given to women at high current fracture risk; prevention aims to maintain bone density so that osteoporosis does not develop later. Bone loss is fastest in the year before and the first years after the final menstrual period (≈10% at the spine and ≈9% at the hip at 5 years, almost 1 T-score unit); abrupt estrogen withdrawal (oophorectomy, stopping MHT) accelerates it. Higher risk: the best predictor is bone density on entering perimenopause — with a T-score <−1.0 most women reach osteoporosis (≤−2.5) before age 65. Risk factors for low BMD: weight <57 kg, prolonged amenorrhea after puberty or delayed puberty (Turner syndrome, exercise-related amenorrhea), previous fracture, family history of osteoporosis, illnesses or drugs that harm the skeleton. Densitometry (DXA): in every perimenopausal woman with any of these factors, to identify those with a T-score <−1.0 who benefit most from prevention. Nutrition, supplements and exercise: advisable for all women, but they do not prevent menopause-related bone loss (calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2, collagen, phytoestrogens and the various exercise regimens at best slow it modestly). Estrogen: oral, transdermal or systemic-dose vaginal MHT prevents bone loss for as long as it is used (also combined with a progestogen or bazedoxifene) and reduces spine and hip fractures by 30–40%. Consider it in women reaching menopause with a T-score <−1.0. Best response in early postmenopause with oral estradiol 2mg or a 0.1mg/day patch; in perimenopause, contraceptives with 20µg ethinyl estradiol are effective. Lower doses protect a smaller proportion of women (the 0.014mg patch was only studied in late postmenopause, ages 60–80). No serum estradiol target has been validated; with transdermal products it can be measured to check absorption. No fixed duration limit; individualize. When estrogen is stopped: the bone benefit is lost within 12 months. Give a bisphosphonate for 2–3 years (alendronate, or one zoledronic acid infusion), then raloxifene or intermittent bisphosphonate to maintain density. If estrogen is contraindicated: approved for prevention are raloxifene (weak effect, does not fully prevent loss) and the bisphosphonates alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate. For prevention, alendronate and zoledronate are used at half the treatment dose: alendronate 35mg PO weekly for 3–5 years, or zoledronic acid 2 doses 2 years apart; then intermittent bisphosphonate. MHT without vasomotor symptoms: The Menopause Society considers it reasonable to prevent bone loss in women at high risk of osteoporosis; the USPSTF (2022) recommends against MHT for the primary prevention of chronic conditions. Use shared decision-making. CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: McClung MR, Clark AL. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 (The Menopause Society) · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025 · USPSTF 2022.

novedades.texto: Folic acid: 400–800 µg/day standard from preconception. 4 mg/day (ACOG) or 5 mg/day (NICE) up to wk 12 with a previous neural tube defect, epilepsy, obesity or diabetes. With MTHFR: standard folic acid (CDC, the only form proven to prevent NTDs); methylfolate 400–800 µg/day as an optional alternative Iron: 30–60 mg/day prophylaxis (WHO). Anaemia: 120 mg/day elemental iron until Hb normalises, then prophylaxis. Hb <7 g/dL: IV iron from the 2nd trimester and consider transfusion according to the clinical picture Calcium: requirement 1000 mg/day (1300 under 19 years), the same as outside pregnancy (IOM 2011). WHO: 1.5–2 g/day in low-intake populations to prevent pre-eclampsia. Cochrane 2025 (Cluver, 10 trials, 37,504 women): no difference in pre-eclampsia in the large trials. Physician's decision; separate from iron Vitamin D: 20–29 ng/mL: supplement at the physician's discretion (1000–2000 IU/day); deficiency <20: 2000–4000 IU/day. Without testing: Endocrine Society 2024 suggests empirical supplementation; WHO 2020, no routine supplementation Omega-3 (DHA): 200–300 mg/day in the general population. With risk of preterm birth: 500–1000 mg/day DHA+EPA before 20 wk (Cochrane 2018: 42% fewer births <34 wk) Iodine: 150 µg/day supplement (potassium iodide) from preconception; total intake target 250 µg/day (ATA). Avoid supplements >500 µg/day
